A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TF-Restormer research despite the changed title and format. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

before.justification: v1 reports original restoration, denoising, super-resolution, streaming and ablation results, including VoxCeleb evaluation in Appendix F.

after.justification: v3 retains original TF-Restormer results and adds dedicated-model evaluations, expanded ablations, and URGENT and DNS benchmark results.

M1.justification: The core architecture, frequency queries, projection, streaming modules and scaled log-spectral loss are retained. v3 adds limited task-specific adaptations, including removal of negligible-power high-frequency bins before URGENT processing and modified loss weights for dedicated training (Appendices F and A.3). The expanded master-query description alone does not establish an architectural change.

E1.justification: v3 retains UNIVERSE, VCTK-DEMAND, clean/noisy-distorted VCTK super-resolution and VoxCeleb coverage, and adds URGENT 2025 blind/non-blind evaluation and DNS 2020 test subsets with and without reverberation. DNS previously supplied training noise; evaluating its challenge test data adds distinct coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds a streaming comparison against NSNet2, DCCRN, FullSubNet+, FRCRN and DeepFilterNet variants on VCTK-DEMAND, plus URGENT and DNS comparator groups including USEM, MFNet, SELM, GenSE and UniSE. Conversely, the retained VoxCeleb comparison drops HiFi++ and BBED (v1 Table 8 versus v3 Table 4(a)).

E3.justification: Tables 1–2 drop WVMOS and SpeechTokenDistance; super-resolution Table 3 replaces MCD/UTMOS reporting with NISQA alongside LSD. v3 also introduces dedicated training regimes, a parameter-matched architecture control, sampling-rate distribution experiments, streaming composite metrics, and DNS subset-specific evaluation. These are substantial protocol additions, while the unified model's stated training budget and original splits remain stable.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's loss, decoder and projection ablations, v3 tests a smaller architecture control, shared versus separate discriminators and projections, perceptual-loss dependence, additional spectral losses and scale choices, and imbalanced sampling-rate exposure (Tables 5–7 and 11). The former decoder-only baseline is renamed encoder-only, rather than newly introduced. The denoising panel of the original loss ablation is removed.

E5.justification: v1 Table 8 reports VoxCeleb scores with uncertainty terms, such as TF-Restormer UTMOS 3.98 ± 0.09. v3 Table 4(a) retains only central values. Neither PDF specifies repeated-run counts or seeds, and v1 does not identify what its ± terms represent.

E6.justification: Most retained unified-model scores remain unchanged, but v3 adds extensive NISQA, dedicated-model, URGENT, DNS, streaming and ablation results. For example, Table 2 adds dedicated-model PESQ 3.63 alongside the retained unified-model 3.41 under different training. Several earlier metric columns and VoxCeleb rows disappear. Appendix H's claimed dedicated-DNS superiority cannot be verified because Table 14 contains no dedicated-model result.

T1.justification: The STFT sampling-rate relation, frequency-projection equations, loss definitions and scaled-log gradient derivation are retained. Explicit query indexing elaborates the existing construction; neither version supplies additional theorems, proofs or substantive mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: v3 retains the principal architectural and training contributions but narrows the abstract's broad assertion that TF-Restormer 'consistently outperforms prior systems' to stable restoration and balanced perceptual quality. Decoupled input-output rates become the central framing, although that capability and novelty claim already appeared in v1.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive qualifications about extension-query undertraining under extreme rate imbalance and the scaled-log loss's dependence on perceptual supervision and appropriate scaling. It also interprets dedicated-training fidelity/perceptual tradeoffs and acknowledges the streaming model's much greater computational cost than lightweight denoisers. These extend v1's existing artifact, language-bias and multi-speaker limitations.

D1.justification: v3 documents master-query slicing, dedicated-training loss weights, additional ablation configuration information and the 2,937-utterance noisy-distorted evaluation set. It removes the explicit pretrained-model/inference-code disclosure, differentiable-PESQ implementation link and VoxCeleb selection details. The general code/demo link and unified-model hardware, optimizer schedules and dimensions are retained.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands engagement with URGENT systems, lightweight streaming enhancement and recent language-model restoration, including LLaSE-G1, UniSE and GenSE. It newly credits SpatialNet when motivating frequency projection and sharing. Older HiFi++, BBED, iSTFTNet and Wave-U-Net references disappear, while comparisons with specialized deterministic systems receive substantially more discussion.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten around decoupled-rate modeling. v3 expands the decoder explanation, reorganizes contributions and ablations, introduces separate additional-evaluation sections, and restructures the appendices. These changes exceed terminology edits or the insertion of new results alone.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch to two columns. v3 removes the separate architecture Figure 2, revises the overview and module diagrams, redistributes the composite ablation table into Tables 5–7, and moves a reduced VoxCeleb table into the main text. Benchmark and sampling-distribution additions introduce several new table layouts.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the design: parameter-controlled architecture comparisons, direct discriminator tests, broader loss controls and sampling-rate sensitivity experiments address weaknesses in v1's component validation. Added benchmark comparisons expose practical costs and fidelity/perceptual tradeoffs, making applicability clearer. These gains outweigh the loss of VoxCeleb uncertainty reporting and remaining reporting defects, notably the dedicated-DNS superiority claim unsupported by Table 14.
